name: Orange juice / vitamin C diet

card.summary: Heavy orange juice or vitamin C intake for skin, resting on vitamin C's collagen role; untested for appearance and sugar-heavy.
card.note: High doses cause GI effects; juice is high in sugar.

quick.overview:
This practice involves taking in large amounts of orange juice or vitamin C for skin. The idea rests on vitamin C's role in collagen formation.

No studies have tested it for appearance, and orange juice is high in sugar.
quick.mechanism: Vitamin C is a cofactor for collagen-building enzymes; whether extra intake beyond adequacy changes skin is untested in this context.
quick.risks: Doses above about 3,000 mg/day have caused diarrhea and other gastrointestinal effects, and the US upper level is 2,000 mg/day.

lead: The orange juice or vitamin C diet is a practice of drinking large amounts of orange or other citrus juice, or raising vitamin C intake generally, with the aim of firmer, brighter-looking skin. The reasoning followers give is that vitamin C is required by the enzymes that build collagen, the protein that gives skin its structure, so keeping intake high is seen as supporting a healthy, glowing complexion [1][2].

Orange juice is a convenient source: a 250 mL cup provides roughly 112 calories, about 21 g of sugar and, by Wikipedia's figure, about 149 percent of the daily value of vitamin C, along with potassium, thiamin and folate [3]. Some community members treat juice as an add-on to protein-heavy or low-carbohydrate eating, while others weigh its vitamin C against its sugar and carbohydrate content [4][5].

Reference sources give the US recommended intake as 90 mg per day for men and 75 mg per day for women. Absorption is close to complete at ordinary intakes and falls at larger single doses, with plasma levels saturating at roughly 100 to 400 mg per day depending on the source [2][1]. No published trial has tested orange-juice-centred protocols for skin appearance; the research that exists concerns vitamin C status and skin biology in general, dietary associations with skin condition, and orange juice in other health contexts [6][15][16].

chain: Higher vitamin C intake from juice or supplements
More vitamin C available for collagen-building enzymes in the skin
angle.text: Followers drink orange juice or raise vitamin C intake hoping for firmer, brighter skin, since vitamin C is a cofactor in collagen formation. Orange juice also adds fluid and citrus flavonoids to the diet.

paras: The practice has no single founder or manual. It appears in nutrition and skin discussions as a general idea: citrus juice or a vitamin C supplement once or several times a day, sometimes alongside other fruit, with firmer and brighter skin as the hoped-for result [4][5]. Variants include fresh-squeezed juice, store-bought not-from-concentrate juice, citrus fruit eaten whole, and vitamin C tablets or powders, with juice sometimes added to a diet otherwise built around meat, dairy and little else [5].
Orange juice is the example participants raise when asking whether a high-volume habit counts as a 'looksmax' [4].

A 250 mL cup of orange juice is about 88 percent water and provides roughly 112 calories, 26 g of carbohydrate (21 g of sugar), 2 g of protein and small amounts of fibre and fat, with moderate potassium, thiamin and folate. Vitamin C is the standout nutrient [3]. Reconstituted frozen orange juice provides about 68 mg of vitamin C per three-quarter cup [1]. Oranges and lemons contain roughly 53 mg per 100 g, and other foods such as acerola, camu camu and kakadu plum contain more; pasteurisation and cooking reduce the content in foods [2].

Orange juice has a pH of about 3.5 because of its citric acid [3]. Wikipedia notes that its health value is debated because it is high in vitamin C but also high in simple sugars comparable to soft drinks, and that some government nutrition advice, such as UK guidance, now favours whole fruit and limiting juice [3]. Producers may add vitamin C to replace what pasteurisation destroys [3].

Vitamin C is a required cofactor for the enzymes that hydroxylate proline and lysine in collagen, and prolonged deficiency causes scurvy, whose features include poor wound healing and skin and gum changes [2][1]. Wikipedia says it was discovered in 1912, isolated in 1928, produced chemically in 1933, and that Albert Szent-Gyorgyi won the 1937 Nobel Prize in part for this work [2]. Skin concentrations of ascorbic acid are lower in older adults in both epidermis and dermis, according to a 2001 study summarised by the Linus Pauling Institute, and UV exposure depletes skin antioxidants including ascorbic acid and vitamin E [6].

The same source notes that the epidermis has no blood supply, so dietary nutrients may reach it slowly, and that topical application can deliver nutrients directly to the epidermis [6]. This is the usual reason skincare uses vitamin C serums as well as, or instead of, oral intake.

A 2017 cross-sectional study of 118 community-dwelling Japanese adults aged 65 and older found that higher habitual vitamin C intake was associated with greater dermal intensity on ultrasound (p=0.017), and that a vegetable- and fruit-rich pattern went with better skin condition; as an observational design it shows association rather than cause [15].

Orange juice also contains flavonoids, and a 2021 editorial reviewed antioxidant and anti-inflammatory properties of orange juice in general [7]. A 2022 scoping review, systematic review and meta-analysis of 21 interventional studies of 100% orange juice reported significantly lower interleukin-6 afterwards and non-significant changes in hs-CRP and malondialdehyde, with the authors urging caution because of moderate risk of bias and small samples [16].

At ordinary intakes active transport absorbs most vitamin C, about 70 to 90 percent at 30 to 180 mg a day, falling below 50 percent at large doses, and the excess is mostly excreted in urine [2][1]. The US upper intake level of 2 g per day was set to avoid gastrointestinal effects such as diarrhea, while the European Food Safety Authority found insufficient evidence to set one [2]. Supplements raise urinary oxalate, and people prone to kidney stones may wish to avoid doses of 1 g or more per day, according to the Linus Pauling Institute [1].

Wikipedia's fruit juice article reports that 100% fruit juice is not associated with higher diabetes risk in research, while sugar-sweetened juice is linked to type 2 diabetes in longitudinal studies, and that a 2018 review linked 100% juice to tooth decay in children while finding no conclusive evidence of other adverse effects [14]. A 2025 umbrella review concluded the evidence did not justify excluding 100% juice from healthy-eating guides, although overconsumption may displace whole fruit [14]. A 2022 meta-analysis of controlled feeding trials reported that 100% fruit juice lowered CRP in substitution trials, with moderate to low certainty [16]. The American Academy of Pediatrics advises limiting juice for ages one to six to about 4 to 6 oz a day [14].

Frozen concentrated orange juice was developed after World War II by the US government and the Florida Department of Citrus after soldiers disliked the vitamin C lemon powder in K-rations; it appeared in 1948, and by 1949 Florida plants produced over 10 million gallons of concentrate. Not-from-concentrate juice followed in the 1990s [3]. Linus Pauling's 1970 book popularised high-dose vitamin C for the common cold, a background to later megadose habits [2].

On looksmax.org orange juice appears in diet threads where members weigh its vitamin C against its sugar content [5], and in light-hearted questions about whether drinking two litres counts as improving looks, with one reply saying 'as long as it's tasty' [4]. One poster describes a low-carbohydrate, high-protein 'carnivore' style diet and asks about adding juice [5].

No studies found on orange-juice-centred diets for skin appearance. Studies of orange juice in other settings include a randomized trial in 40 young adults aged 18 to 29 with major depressive disorder comparing flavonoid-rich orange juice with a flavonoid-low orange cordial [8], a randomized trial of daily orange consumption in fatty liver disease [9], a randomized trial of beverages and hydration status [10], a trial of Moro orange juice for weight management [11] and a study of orange juice intake and anthropometric changes in children and adolescents [12]. None examined skin.

The US Institute of Medicine set a 2,000 mg per day upper level in 2000 based on gastrointestinal effects seen above 3,000 mg per day [2]. Wikipedia lists stomach discomfort, headache, sleep problems and skin flushing as possible effects of large doses [2]. Orange juice is acidic and sugar-rich, and fruit acids can erode enamel when juice is overconsumed [3][14]. A review has described interactions between fruit juices other than grapefruit and some drugs [13].

timeline.event: Flash pasteurisation developed, fixing an early metallic taste in canned juice [3].
Vitamin C becomes the first vitamin produced chemically [2].
Albert Szent-Gyorgyi awarded the Nobel Prize in part for vitamin C work [2].
Frozen concentrated orange juice appears after wartime development of a vitamin C drink for soldiers [3].
Linus Pauling promotes vitamin C for the common cold in a book [2].
US Institute of Medicine sets a 2,000 mg per day vitamin C upper level [2].
Cross-sectional study links higher vitamin C intake to better dermal ultrasound intensity in older adults [15].
Meta-analysis of 100% orange juice trials reports lower interleukin-6 [16].

lore.intro: Online, citrus and vitamin C are discussed for brighter skin, with members debating juice against whole foods and supplements [5][4].

claims.claim: High vitamin C or orange juice intake improves skin quality
claims.believers: Proponents cite vitamin C's role in collagen synthesis [2].
claims.experts: Reference works describe vitamin C's collagen role and note that absorption saturates; no studies of juice-based protocols for skin were found [2][1].

claims.claim: Orange juice is mostly sugar with little nutritional value
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread participant describes juice as largely sugar with a low amount of vitamin C [5].
claims.experts: A cup contains about 21 g of sugar and is a rich source of vitamin C; Wikipedia describes its health value as debated [3].

claims.claim: Drinking a lot of juice every day is a 'looksmax'
claims.believers: A looksmax.org thread asks if two litres of orange juice daily is a looksmax or looksmin; replies range from 'as long as it's tasty' to calling it a coping habit [4].
claims.experts: No published study links juice volume to appearance outcomes; guidance in some countries favours whole fruit over juice [3].

claims.claim: Orange juice can be added to a low-carb or carnivore diet
claims.believers: One looksmax.org poster who eats low-carbohydrate, high-protein is thinking of adding juice but is hesitant about the sugar [5].
claims.experts: Wikipedia reports that juice is high in simple sugars [3]; no study has tested juice within carnivore-style diets for appearance.

claims.claim: Vitamin C intake is linked to better skin condition
claims.believers: Proponents point to vitamin C's role in collagen [2].
claims.experts: A 2017 cross-sectional study found higher intake associated with greater dermal intensity in older adults, an association rather than a trial [15].
